result:
There's something quietly remarkable about handwriting that we're only beginning to notice now that it's disappearing. Each person's script is a kind of accidental self-portrait—the way someone crosses their t's, whether their letters lean forward eagerly or stand upright with caution, how the pressure of the pen betrays mood and haste and care. A grocery list written at 7 a.m. tells you more about a person than they might intend.

Graphologists have made pseudoscientific claims about what handwriting reveals, but the truth is stranger: your handwriting doesn't reveal a fixed personality so much as a moment of one. Compare letters you wrote at fifteen to ones you write today. The loops have tightened or loosened; the slant has shifted. You changed, and your hand recorded it without asking permission.

Before typewriters and keyboards, everything human passed through the hand first. Love letters, treaties, recipes, confessions—all of them carried the tremor of the body that made them. When we read an old letter, part of what moves us isn't just the words but the evidence of effort: ink blots where the pen rested too long, crossed-out words preserved rather than deleted, the way lines drift downward as fatigue sets in near midnight.

Digital text is democratic and clean, and I wouldn't trade it back. But there's a loss in perfect reproducibility. Every message looks identical regardless of who typed it or when. Somewhere in that uniformity, we traded the trace of ourselves for convenience—a fair bargain, probably, but worth mourning a little.

- The nature of language
- A small observation about everyday life
